title: Sea Turtles: Long Journeys Home
summary: How sea turtles travel across the ocean back to the beach where they hatched, lay their eggs, and face dangers that people can help reduce.
poll: People should keep beaches dark at night to help sea turtles.

versions.title: Sea Turtles Go Home
versions.text:
This is a sea turtle. It lives in the sea. It is a reptile. It has a hard shell. It swims with big, flat legs. They are called flippers. It needs air. So it swims up to breathe.

A sea turtle can make a long trip. This trip is a journey. A mom turtle swims back to the beach where she was born. It is far. How does she find it? The Earth helps her. It is like a map in her head.

At night, she digs a nest in the sand. She lays lots of eggs. It can be 100 eggs! She fills the hole with sand. Then she goes back to the sea.

Warm sand makes more girls. Cool sand makes more boys.

In two months, the eggs hatch. Each baby is a hatchling. The babies dig out at night. They crawl to the bright sea. Birds and crabs eat lots of them. Few grow up.

In Saudi Arabia, sea turtles nest on the Red Sea coast. They nest on Gulf islands, too.

Turtles need help. A plastic bag can look like food. Keep the beach clean. Keep it dark at night.

versions.title: Sea Turtles Go Home
versions.text:
Sea turtles live in the sea. A sea turtle is a reptile. It has a hard shell on its back. It swims with four flat legs called flippers. It breathes air, so it swims up to the top for a breath.

Sea turtles make long trips. A long trip is called a journey. A mother turtle swims back to the beach where she hatched. She may swim a very long way. How does she know the way? Scientists think the Earth helps her. It works like a map that she can feel.

At night, she crawls up on the sand. She digs a deep hole for a nest. She lays about 100 eggs in it. Then she covers the eggs with sand. She goes back to the sea and does not come back for them.

The sand keeps the eggs warm. Warm sand makes more girls. Cool sand makes more boys.

After about two months, the eggs hatch. Each baby is called a hatchling. The babies dig out at night. They crawl to the sea, which looks bright. Birds, crabs, and fish eat many of them. Only a few grow up.

In Saudi Arabia, sea turtles nest on beaches by the Red Sea. They also nest on small islands in the Gulf.

Sea turtles need help. A plastic bag in the sea can look like a jellyfish. A turtle may eat it and get sick. We can keep beaches clean and dark at night.

versions.title: Sea Turtles: The Long Trip Home
versions.text:
Sea turtles spend most of their lives in the ocean. A sea turtle is a reptile, like a lizard or a snake. It has a hard shell. It has four flat flippers for swimming. It breathes air, so it must swim to the top to take a breath.

Sea turtles are known for their long trips. Each trip is a journey across the sea. When a female turtle is grown, she swims back to the beach where she hatched. That was many years before! She may swim thousands of kilometers to get there. Scientists think turtles can feel the pull of the Earth. It helps them find their way like a map.

On a dark night, the mother turtle crawls onto the sand. She digs a deep nest with her back flippers. She lays about 100 round eggs. Then she covers them with sand and goes back to the sea. She never comes back to see her babies.

The warmth of the sand matters. Warm sand makes more female turtles. Cool sand makes more males.

About two months later, the eggs hatch. Each baby turtle is called a hatchling. The tiny hatchlings dig out at night. They crawl to the ocean because it looks brighter than the land. Birds, crabs, and fish eat many of them. Only about one in a thousand grows up.

In Saudi Arabia, green turtles and hawksbill turtles nest on beaches by the Red Sea. They also nest on islands in the Arabian Gulf.

Sea turtles face many dangers. A plastic bag in the sea can look like a jellyfish. A turtle may eat it. People can help. They can keep beaches clean and dark at night.

versions.title: Sea Turtles: The Long Trip Home
versions.text:
Sea turtles spend almost their whole lives in the ocean. A sea turtle is a reptile. It is related to lizards and snakes. It has a hard shell and four strong flippers instead of feet. Like all reptiles, it breathes air. It must come up to the surface to take a breath.

Sea turtles are famous for their long journeys. When a female turtle is grown, she swims back to the beach where she hatched. She left it many years earlier. Some turtles travel thousands of kilometers to get there. Scientists think turtles can feel the pull of the Earth. This helps them find their way, like a map they can feel.

On a dark night, the mother turtle crawls up onto the sand. She uses her back flippers to dig a deep nest. She lays about 100 eggs that look like small white balls. Then she covers them with sand and returns to the sea. She never comes back to care for her young.

The warmth of the sand decides something surprising. Warm sand makes more female turtles, and cooler sand makes more males.

About two months later, the eggs hatch. Each baby turtle is called a hatchling. The hatchlings dig out, usually at night. They crawl toward the ocean because it looks brighter than the land. Birds, crabs, and fish eat many of them. Only about one hatchling in a thousand lives to become an adult.

In Saudi Arabia, green turtles and hawksbill turtles nest on beaches along the Red Sea. They also nest on islands in the Arabian Gulf.

Sea turtles face many dangers. A floating plastic bag can look like a jellyfish. A hungry turtle may swallow it. People can help by keeping beaches clean and dark at night.

versions.title: Sea Turtles: Long Journeys Home
versions.text:
Sea turtles spend nearly their whole lives in the ocean. They are reptiles, related to lizards and snakes. They have hard shells and powerful flippers instead of feet. Like other reptiles, they breathe air, so they must come up to the surface for a breath.

Sea turtles are known for their long journeys. Many of them migrate, which means they travel a long way between the places where they feed and the places where they nest. When a female is fully grown, she returns to the same beach where she hatched many years before. Some turtles swim thousands of kilometers to get there. How do they navigate across the open sea? Scientists believe turtles can sense the Earth's magnetic field. It works like an invisible map that guides them home.

On a dark night, the mother turtle crawls slowly onto the sand. With her back flippers, she digs a deep nest and lays about 100 eggs. She covers them with sand and returns to the sea. She never comes back to care for her young.

The temperature of the sand decides something surprising. Warmer sand produces more female turtles, while cooler sand produces more males.

After about two months, the eggs hatch. The tiny hatchlings dig their way out, usually at night. They crawl toward the ocean because the sky above the water looks brighter than the land. Many never reach the waves. Birds and crabs catch them on the beach, and fish wait in the water. These predators are so common that only about one hatchling in a thousand grows up.

In Saudi Arabia, green turtles and hawksbill turtles nest on beaches along the Red Sea and on islands in the Arabian Gulf, such as Karan and Jana.

Sea turtles also face dangers caused by people. Bright lights on a beach can confuse hatchlings, so they crawl the wrong way. A floating plastic bag can look like a jellyfish, and a turtle may swallow it. Keeping beaches clean and dark can help them survive.

versions.title: Sea Turtles: Long Journeys Home
versions.text:
Although sea turtles spend nearly their entire lives in the ocean, they are not fish but reptiles, closely related to lizards and snakes. They possess protective shells and powerful flippers instead of feet, and because they breathe air, they must regularly return to the surface between dives.

Sea turtles are celebrated for their extraordinary journeys. Many species migrate across enormous distances, moving between the coastal waters where they feed and the beaches where they nest. When a female reaches adulthood, which may take twenty years or more, she typically returns to the same beach where she hatched, sometimes swimming thousands of kilometers to reach it. Her navigation across the featureless open ocean remains one of nature's great puzzles, but scientists believe sea turtles can detect the Earth's magnetic field, which functions like an invisible map guiding them home. No adult teaches a young turtle this route, so the ability must depend on instinct.

On a dark night, the female crawls laboriously up the beach. With her back flippers, she excavates a deep chamber and deposits approximately 100 leathery eggs. She covers the nest carefully with sand and returns to the sea, never coming back to care for her offspring.

The warm sand now begins to incubate the eggs, and its temperature determines something remarkable. Warmer sand produces more female hatchlings, while cooler sand produces more males, a fact that worries researchers as global temperatures rise.

After approximately two months of incubation, the eggs hatch, and the tiny turtles struggle to the surface, usually at night. They crawl toward the ocean because the horizon above the water appears brighter than the land behind them. This brief trip is extremely hazardous, since birds and crabs hunt them on the sand and hungry fish wait in the shallows. Consequently, only about one hatchling in a thousand survives to adulthood.

In Saudi Arabia, green turtles and hawksbill turtles nest along the Red Sea coast and on islands in the Arabian Gulf, including Karan and Jana.

Today, several sea turtle species are endangered, largely because of human activity. Artificial lights near beaches can lure hatchlings inland, away from the water. Floating plastic bags resemble jellyfish, and turtles that swallow them can become seriously ill. Conservation efforts, such as protecting nesting beaches, keeping them dark at night, and removing plastic, significantly improve the turtles' chances of survival.

versions.title: Sea Turtles: Long Journeys Home
versions.text:
Although sea turtles spend virtually their entire lives in the ocean, they are not fish but reptiles, closely related to lizards and snakes, and they possess protective carapaces and powerful flippers rather than feet. Because they breathe atmospheric oxygen, they must periodically return to the surface between their remarkably lengthy dives.

Sea turtles are renowned for their extraordinary journeys. Numerous species migrate across enormous distances, traveling between the coastal feeding grounds where they spend most of the year and the particular beaches where they reproduce. When a female reaches maturity, which may require twenty years or more, she characteristically returns to the same beach where she originally hatched, occasionally swimming thousands of kilometers to reach it. Her navigation across the featureless open ocean remains one of nature's most intriguing mysteries, but scientists hypothesize that sea turtles can detect the Earth's magnetic field, which functions like an invisible map directing them toward their destination. Because no adult ever teaches a juvenile turtle this route, the ability must depend on instinct rather than on learning or accumulated experience.

On a moonless night, the female crawls laboriously up the beach. With her back flippers, she excavates a deep chamber and deposits approximately 100 leathery eggs, which she covers meticulously with sand before returning to the sea, never coming back to care for her offspring.

The surrounding sand subsequently begins to incubate the eggs, and its temperature determines something remarkable: warmer sand produces predominantly female hatchlings, whereas cooler sand produces predominantly males, a phenomenon that worries researchers as global temperatures rise.

After approximately two months of incubation, the eggs hatch, and the tiny turtles struggle collectively to the surface, usually under the protective cover of darkness. They instinctively crawl toward the ocean because the horizon above the water appears brighter than the vegetation and dunes behind them. This brief expedition is extraordinarily hazardous, since birds and crabs hunt them on the sand while predatory fish patrol the shallows. Consequently, only approximately one hatchling in a thousand survives to adulthood.

In Saudi Arabia, green turtles and hawksbill turtles nest along the Red Sea coastline and on islands in the Arabian Gulf, including Karan and Jana.

Today, several sea turtle species are officially classified as endangered, predominantly as a consequence of human activity. Artificial illumination near beaches can lure disoriented hatchlings inland, away from the water. Floating plastic bags resemble jellyfish, and turtles that swallow them can become seriously ill. As a set of questions and answers that a scientist asks about turtles
In time order, following a turtle's life from the nest to the sea
questions.why: The article moves step by step: the mother returns, digs a nest, the eggs hatch after two months, and the hatchlings crawl to the sea.

wrong.A: The facts follow a clear order through the turtle's life.
wrong.B: The article says turtles are not fish but does not compare them throughout.
wrong.C: There is one question about navigation, but the article is not built as questions and answers.

MID.prompt: Explain two dangers that hatchlings face and how people can help reduce one of them. Use details from the article.
checklist: I explained two dangers with details from the article.
I described one way people can help.
I used at least two key words correctly.
MID.modelAnswer: One danger hatchlings face is predators, since birds and crabs hunt them on the sand and fish wait for them in the shallow water, which is why only about one in a thousand survives. A second danger is plastic pollution, because a floating plastic bag looks like a jellyfish and a turtle that swallows one can become very sick. People can help reduce this second danger by keeping beaches clean so there is less trash for sea turtles to mistake for food.

keyWords.definition: a way of acting that an animal is born knowing, without being taught
keyWords.example: A spider builds its web by instinct, not because another spider showed it how.

keyWords.definition: the skill or act of finding a route from one place to another
keyWords.example: Modern ships use satellite navigation to cross the ocean safely.

keyWords.definition: to keep eggs warm so they can develop and hatch
keyWords.example: The farmer used a warm box to incubate the chicken eggs.

keyWords.definition: at risk of dying out completely
keyWords.example: The Arabian leopard is endangered, so scientists work hard to protect it.

keyWords.definition: the careful protection of nature, animals, and natural places
keyWords.example: Our school joined a conservation project to plant mangrove trees.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Sea turtles complete remarkable journeys guided by instinct, but their survival now depends partly on human choices.
Sea turtles are fish that rarely leave the ocean.
Sea turtle eggs always produce equal numbers of males and females, no matter how warm the sand is.
Sea turtles are no longer found near Saudi Arabia.
questions.why: The article describes the turtles' instinctive navigation and nesting, then explains that species are endangered and conservation helps them survive.

wrong.B: The article states they are reptiles, not fish.
wrong.C: Sand temperature changes the balance of males and females.
wrong.D: The article says green and hawksbill turtles nest in Saudi Arabia.

questions.stem: According to the article, how long may it take a female sea turtle to reach maturity?
options: About two months
About one year after hatching
Twenty years or more
One hundred years or longer
questions.why: The article says reaching maturity may require twenty years or more.

wrong.A: Two months is how long the eggs incubate.
wrong.B: The article gives a much longer time.
wrong.D: The article does not give this number.

questions.stem: Which places in or near Saudi Arabia does the article name as turtle nesting sites?
options: The Empty Quarter dunes
The Red Sea coast and Gulf islands such as Karan and Jana
Rivers and streams in the Asir mountains of the south
Lakes near Riyadh
questions.why: The article says green and hawksbill turtles nest along the Red Sea coast and on Arabian Gulf islands, including Karan and Jana.

wrong.A: Turtles nest on beaches by the sea, not in desert dunes.

questions.stem: In the article, the sand "begins to incubate the eggs." What does incubate mean here?
options: To bury something so animals cannot find it
To wash something with seawater
To count and record
To keep eggs warm while they develop
questions.why: After the mother leaves, the warm sand keeps the eggs warm for about two months until they hatch.

wrong.A: The sand covers the eggs, but incubate is about warmth and development.
wrong.B: Seawater is not part of incubation.
wrong.C: Counting is not what the sand does.

questions.stem: Why does the author conclude that turtle navigation "must depend on instinct"?
options: Because no adult ever teaches a young turtle the route
Because turtles travel in large groups
Because scientists have trained young turtles to follow maps
Because turtles always nest on the nearest beach
questions.why: The mother leaves before her eggs hatch, so the young cannot learn the route from an adult; the ability must be inborn.

wrong.B: The article does not describe group travel.
wrong.C: No one trains turtles to use maps.
wrong.D: Females return to the beach where they hatched, which may be thousands of kilometers away.

questions.stem: The article says scientists are worried as global temperatures rise. Which detail best explains this concern?
options: Warm water makes adult turtles swim much more slowly, so their long journeys take many extra years.
Hatchlings crawl toward bright horizons.
Warmer sand produces mostly female hatchlings, which could upset the balance of males and females.
Plastic bags look like jellyfish.
questions.why: Because sand temperature decides whether hatchlings are female or male, hotter beaches could produce too few males.

wrong.B: This is true but is not linked to rising temperatures.
wrong.D: This is a danger, but it is not about temperature.

questions.stem: What is the effect of artificial lights near a nesting beach?
options: They help mothers find the beach.
They lure hatchlings inland, away from the water.
They warm the eggs in the sand and speed up hatching.
They keep predators away from the nests.
questions.why: Hatchlings move toward the brightest horizon, so lights on land can lead them away from the sea.

wrong.A: Mothers navigate with the magnetic field, not lights.
wrong.C: The article does not link lights to hatching speed.
wrong.D: The article does not say lights scare predators.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe the dangers of lights and plastic before mentioning conservation efforts?
options: To prove that turtles cannot survive at all
To show that every one of the problems has already been solved
To compare turtles with jellyfish
To show the problems first, so the solutions make sense
questions.why: The last paragraph uses a problem-and-solution structure: it names the human-made dangers, then explains how conservation answers them.

wrong.A: The author says conservation improves their chances, so survival is possible.
wrong.B: The species are still endangered, so the problems remain.
wrong.C: Jellyfish are mentioned only because plastic bags look like them.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how a sea turtle's life cycle makes it both remarkable and vulnerable. Use evidence about navigation, incubation, and human activity.
checklist: I explained at least one remarkable ability and one danger.
I supported my ideas with specific details from the article.
I used at least three key words accurately.
HIGH.modelAnswer: A sea turtle's life cycle is remarkable because of its instinct for navigation: scientists believe it can sense Earth's magnetic field like an invisible map, which lets a female migrate thousands of kilometers back to the very beach where she once hatched. The same life cycle also makes the species vulnerable, since the incubation of the eggs depends on sand temperature, which determines whether more males or females hatch, and the long dangerous journey from nest to sea leaves hatchlings easy prey for birds, crabs, and fish. Because threats such as plastic pollution and bright beachside lights add to these natural dangers, conservation efforts like keeping beaches dark and clean are essential to the turtles' survival.
